title: Ops control & fallback playbook vs hyperscaler managed endpoints
content:
Executive summary

This is a tactical playbook for positioning Redwood Inference against hyperscaler managed endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure). Focus: operational control, predictable unit economics, and graceful degradation. The goal is to give field teams concise scripts, discovery questions, technical proof points, and quick rebuttals for the most common hyperscaler objections.

Target buyer personas

- Platform/Infra Leads (SRE, Platform Eng): care about repeatability, SLA, observability, and incident remediation windows.
- ML/Model Ops: prioritize model versioning, rollout control, and reproducible inference stacks.
- App/Product Engineers: want latency, cost predictability, and minimal integration friction.
- Security/Compliance: data residency, KMS/HSM controls, audit logs, air-gapped options.

Top-level win themes (short pitches)

1) Deterministic ops control
 - Pitch: Redwood gives you configuration-level control over routing, fallbacks, and quantization profiles. You control which model variant serves which traffic slices.
 - Why it matters: Hyperscalers trade off control for convenience. Ops teams lose granular routing and rollback primitives.

2) Predictable unit economics and lower tail costs
 - Pitch: Our Optimize toolkit surfaces batching, cache, and quantization levers linked to per-token cost and latency SLOs.
 - Why it matters: Managed endpoints hide variability in cold starts, multi-tenant noisy neighbors, and burst pricing. We make math reproducible for finance.

3) Graceful degradation and multi-tier fallback
 - Pitch: Redwood supports automated fallback rules by latency, cost, region, and model fidelity. If a premium model misses the SLA, traffic falls back to a compatible cached variant automatically.
 - Why it matters: Keeps revenue-critical flows live during provider or model incidents.

4) Private & hybrid deployment parity
 - Pitch: Same API, same rollout semantics across hosted, dedicated, and private. No re-architecture to move workloads off the cloud.
 - Why it matters: Security/constrained customers can move without swapping toolchains.

Field playbook: discovery questions (fast)

- What are your 95/99th percentile latency SLOs for customer-facing paths today?
- How predictable is your per-token cost over a monthly billing cycle? Where do spikes come from?
- Do you have a documented rollback policy for model deployments and routing rules?
- How do you handle cross-region outages or model-specific regressions?
- What telemetry do you need to debug an expensive inference spike (token-level breakdown, route-level tracing)?
- Are you allowed to bring keys to a cloud vendor KMS or use an HSM?

Demo hooks and quick wins to show in 30 minutes

- Live trace: Show token-level cost/latency breakdown for a burst test vs a hyperscaler endpoint. Highlight tail latency and causal link to batching/cold-starts.
- Fallback policy simulation: Run a controlled canary that triggers automatic fallback to a quantized variant and show zero downtime switchover in the dashboard.
- Cost-sensitivity slider: Use Optimize suggestions to toggle batching/kv-cache and show projected cost savings.

Common hyperscaler objections and rebuttals

1) Objection: We already have the managed endpoint, one bill, less operational overhead.
 Rebuttal: For early use cases that works. At scale, the hidden costs are tail latency, platform-wide incident impact, and opaque per-token variability. We buy back ops time with deterministic rollouts, lower tail costs, and clearer incident triage. Offer: propose a 60-day integration pilot on non-critical traffic to quantify tail and cost delta.

2) Objection: Hyperscalers have the best integration with their cloud services.
 Rebuttal: We integrate with cloud infra and marketplaces but keep the control plane independent. Customers can use existing cloud storage, IAM, and monitoring while running inference on Redwood for better SLOs.

3) Objection: How do you handle scale vs their elastic autoscaling?
 Rebuttal: Our Dedicated pools have predictable throughput and configurable burst tiers. For unpredictable spikes we recommend routing policies that spill to hosted capacity while maintaining provenance and audit trails.

Technical proof points to call out

- Kernel selection and quantization profiles that reduce GPU-hours for common LLMs by 20-40% in our benchmarks.
- Automatic KV/prefix caching that reduces per-request tokens by up to 60% for multi-turn chat flows.
- Built-in rollout primitives: canary by user cohort, automatic rollback on metric regressions, and A/B split with traffic shaping.
- Token-level observability: per-route token counts, batching statistics, and tail-latency origin traces.

Quick ROI sketch (sales talking numbers)

- Example customer: 10 million tokens/day, 30% chat reuse, current managed endpoint cost X. With caching + batching we typically show 18-30% cost reduction on token spend and a 40% reduction in tail latency events that cause SLO violations. Translate to saved engineering time and avoided revenue loss during degradation.

Battlecard snippets for AE/SE

- 1-line close: Keep the convenience of a managed interface, gain deterministic ops control and predictable economics.
- 30s pitch for execs: Your core risk isn't access to models, it's keeping critical LLM features online with predictable costs and clear rollback story.
- When to escalate to Solutions Eng: if the customer requires private KMS, air-gap, or on-prem packaging within 90 days.

Tactics around procurement and procurement objections

- Offer a phased commitment: start with Hosted API for experimentation, migrate hot paths to Dedicated capacity, then move regulated flows to Private if required.
- Help procurement build SLAs that map to incident playbooks and rollback windows.

Open questions & next actions (work-in-progress)

- Need a short technical appendix comparing default autoscaling and pricing models across the three major clouds with sample bills. Assigned: Jonas, due 2024-10-18.
- Create a one-page customer-facing ROI calculator with inputs for tokens/day, chat reuse, desired p99 latency. Assigned: Priya, due 2024-10-11.
- Validate the fallback demo on a real enterprise dataset and capture a reproducible script. Assigned: Ethan, due 2024-10-04.

Notes to self and reminders

- Keep the demo deterministic: seed prompts and user cohorts.
- Avoid calling out specific hyperscaler outages in public collateral; stick to generic risks and measurable differences.
- Collect customer quotes that emphasize ops pain rather than model quality.

End.
